The Shortest Path Problem. The task of finding a path between two vertices in a graph such that the sum of the weights of its edges is minimized. Solvable in polynomial time, it stands in striking contrast to the NP-complete traveling salesman problem. Shortest path algorithms are critical to modern technology, powering network routing protocols, GPS navigation systems, and artificial intelligence pathfinding.

Dijkstra's algorithm is the standard method for finding the shortest path from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a graph with non-negative edge weights. It achieves a runtime of O of E plus V log V using a Fibonacci heap, where E is the number of edges and V is the number of vertices.

The Bellman-Ford algorithm handles graphs with negative edge weights and is capable of detecting negative-weight cycles. A negative-weight cycle would otherwise allow an algorithm to loop infinitely to continuously decrease path cost. This makes Bellman-Ford more versatile but slower than Dijkstra's in the non-negative case.

The Floyd-Warshall algorithm is a dynamic programming method that solves the all-pairs shortest path problem—finding shortest paths between all pairs of vertices—in O of V cubed time. This is useful when you need the shortest path between every possible pair of vertices rather than from a single source.

The A-star search algorithm is a heuristic-guided extension of Dijkstra's algorithm that uses estimates of the remaining distance to prune the search space. It is commonly used in video games for pathfinding and in robotics for motion planning. Because the shortest path problem is solvable in polynomial time, it resides within the complexity class P. This distinguishes it fundamentally from NP-hard routing problems. It connects to sorting algorithms through Dijkstra's use of a priority queue, which leverages sorting structures to quickly find the minimum-distance vertex. The all-pairs shortest path problem can also be solved algebraically using tropical semiring matrix multiplication.
